claims.text: Monte Carlo–based chemical short-range ordering can produce HfTi and TiZr clustering in HfNbTaTiZr.
HfTi and TiZr clusters form percolating pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
Including CSRO will predict lattice heat transport more accurately than DFT-based or analytical random-alloy models.
The relevant earlier DFT-based or analytical models assume a fully random solid solution.
The target material is a nominally single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy with less than 1 wt.% oxygen and minimal extrinsic defects.
The initial atomic distribution is random before ordering develops.
A Monte Carlo-generated CSRO structure can be coupled to lattice-dynamics calculations to predict the phonon contribution to thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach is applicable from approximately 200 K to 1200 K.
HfTi and TiZr cluster formation and percolation modulate phonon scattering.
HfTi and TiZr clustering reduces lattice thermal conductivity relative to a fully random alloy.
Clustering creates local regions with altered force constants.
The altered local force constants increase phonon scattering and thereby reduce lattice heat transport.
Explicitly modeling CSRO permits lattice conduction to be separated from electronic conduction.
The CSRO-aware model will predict lattice thermal conductivity approximately 20–30% below estimates from random-alloy models.
Previous models have prediction errors exceeding 30%.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error to approximately 10% in the intrinsic, defect-free regime.
Earlier DFT-derived and analytical estimates combine lattice and electronic contributions and neglect CSRO.
The predicted improvement is limited to single-phase samples containing less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The approach may not be valid above 1200 K because of additional high-temperature effects or multiphase behavior.
The hypothesis is falsified if lattice thermal conductivity differs from the CSRO-model prediction by more than ±10%, or if HfTi and TiZr clustering is absent, across the tested temperature range.
